stories.headline: Report: a family text on her sister’s seized phone led to the Ilhan Omar raid, and agents pulled DNA from her trash beforehand
stories.summary: A family text message found on the phone of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s sister is what got a federal judge to approve Monday’s raid on Omar’s Washington home, according to a New York Times report cited by the New York Post. Investigators seized the phone of Sahra Noor, who now lives in Kenya, earlier this year as they looked into whether the Somalia-born congresswoman conspired to commit immigration fraud when her family came to the U.S. in 1995. The texts were used to get the warrant for the Department of Homeland Security search, in which agents took Omar’s phone, passport, notebooks and computers. Separately, NewsNation reports that federal agents went through Omar’s trash before the raid to collect her DNA. The evidence is expected to go to a federal grand jury in Minnesota to decide whether Omar and her family lied about who they were when they were admitted as refugees after Somalia’s civil war. Omar says she was naturalized in 2000 at 17 through her father, who sources have told the Post misrepresented his identity. Noor canceled a book event in Rochester on Thursday, citing a “family emergency.” Omar’s spokeswoman called the probe “politically motivated” and part of Trump’s “personal vendetta” against her.

stories.headline: A 6-year-old boy and a man are killed after a woman drives a truck through a youth soccer game in Wichita
stories.summary: A 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man were killed and 10 other people were hurt Saturday afternoon when a woman drove a truck through a youth soccer game at the city-run Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas, police said. The 34-year-old driver, from Garden City, Kansas, is in custody and has been cooperative, but police said it was not yet clear whether the crash was intentional. 911 calls started just before 3:30 p.m. Both people who died were from McPherson but were not related. The injured include five children ages 5 to 9 and five adults ages 28 to 68, with injuries ranging from bruises to “extremely severe,” though none are believed to be life-threatening. When officers arrived, the driver was still in the truck with two children, and bystanders were giving first aid to the injured. One of the woman’s children had a game on a different field at the complex. The city canceled all events at the 11-field facility, and the state high school association suspended its flag football state championship and other matches this weekend. Police asked anyone with video to upload it for investigators.

stories.headline: France erupts in riots and looting as more than 1,200 are arrested and Limoges’ 143-year-old town hall burns
stories.summary: Violence broke out in cities across France on Saturday during the latest day of protests over the cost of living and run-down schools, the BBC reports. The government said at least 1,200 people were arrested as an estimated 550,000 took to the streets, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were hurt. In Paris, riot police used tear gas and water cannon into the evening as groups set fires, torched cars around the Place de la République, ransacked shops and gutted at least one restaurant. In Limoges, a fire at the historic town hall caused part of the roof to collapse. Lyon’s historic tourist office was burned, and police said “hostile individuals” kept firefighters from safely reaching it. In Saint-Étienne, the mayor said a young man had his hand blown off by a grenade. An Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied, and masked men drove a tourist train toward riot police in Grenoble. The interior ministry blamed “hooded individuals” for targeted violence in Paris, Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and other cities. Students have protested for weeks over staff shortages and run-down high schools, and on Saturday they were joined by unions and the “yellow vest” movement, as France heads toward an April presidential election with President Macron leaving office.

stories.headline: Report: Kyle Dubas is ready to trade Penguins veterans for picks and prospects to make room for the kids
stories.summary: The Penguins are willing to move a veteran forward for draft picks or prospects to open lineup spots for their young players, Sportsnet’s Elliotte Friedman reported during Saturday’s Hockey Night in Canada. “Pittsburgh has made it clear that they would move a veteran forward for draft picks or prospects to give their younger players more opportunity as they continue to transition to a younger roster,” Friedman said. General manager Kyle Dubas has a group of young players waiting, including Harrison Brunicke and Rutger McGroarty in Wilkes-Barre/Scranton and Ville Koivunen and Hendrix Lapierre, who have been rotating in and out of the lineup. Pittsburgh Hockey Now says the veterans who would bring the biggest returns are winger Bryan Rust, 34, and Rickard Rakell, 33. Defenseman Erik Karlsson is on an expiring contract and has long made clear that winning a Stanley Cup is his priority. Summer signings Andrei Kuzmenko, 30, and Trevor van Riemsdyk, 35, would not bring back much in a trade. The report came as the Penguins played in Vegas Saturday night.

stories.headline: Large fires and explosions light up St. Petersburg as Ukraine launches a big overnight drone attack on Russia’s second city
stories.summary: Ukraine launched what monitoring channels called a “massive” drone attack on St. Petersburg early Sunday local time, with large fires and explosions reported across the city, the Kyiv Independent reports. The attack began around 2:50 a.m. Eyewitness video from residents shows drones flying over the city and air defenses firing, with blasts lighting up the night sky over the city of 5.6 million, about 530 miles north of Ukraine’s border. Leningrad Oblast Gov. Aleksandr Drozdenko said 57 drones were shot down in the region and that debris damaged four cars in a parking lot and started a fire. Ukrainian monitoring channels said port facilities, oil tankers and a data center were targeted and that fires appeared to be burning at several sites. The St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, in the city’s port, is one of Russia’s largest fuel storage and export facilities, handling a reported 12.5 million tons a year; Ukraine hit it on July 4. The Kyiv Independent said it could not independently confirm the targets or damage. Ukraine has also disrupted air traffic and hit data centers around Moscow with drone swarms in recent days.

stories.headline: More than 500 Connecticut National Guard soldiers come home from a nine-month Middle East deployment focused on drone and missile threats
stories.summary: Connecticut welcomed home the Army National Guard’s 1st Battalion, 102nd Infantry Regiment on Saturday with a ceremony at the State Armory in Hartford hosted by Gov. Ned Lamont and the lieutenant governor. More than 500 Connecticut soldiers deployed for nine months to seven countries and 22 locations as tensions with Iran stayed high. Maj. Ross Alexander, a 24-year veteran, said the unit focused on anti-drone and ballistic missile threats, very different from the close combat he saw in Afghanistan. “Two different types of wars,” he said. “This is a completely new experience.” Soldiers received deployment awards at the ceremony, including 46 Bronze Stars and six Purple Hearts. “These guys handled it great. Couldn’t be proud of them,” Alexander said. First Sgt. Brian Shattuck noted that many of the soldiers are also teachers, police officers and coaches who will go back to serving their communities at home.

stories.headline: Sam Altman says OpenAI will build a humanoid robot, with a “cool demo” in 2027, but the hard part is the brain
stories.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the company will build a humanoid robot. Asked on the Sources podcast whether OpenAI would actually make one, he said, “We will,” explaining that a human shape makes sense because “the world is very much designed for people,” from doors to keyboards to tools. Altman said what the robot looks like is “less important than really figuring out … the brain that makes the robot work.” He told Fortune he expects “a cool demo in 2027” but doesn’t think robots will be “walking the streets for a few years longer.” OpenAI hasn’t said what the demo will show or what the robot will look like. Engadget notes the company now lists 27 robotics job openings, covering motion control, custom motors and actuators, manufacturing and supply chain, so the hardware is getting real attention. One posting says the short-term goal is general-purpose robots that help skilled workers build infrastructure, with a personal home robot as the long-term aim. OpenAI would be entering a field where Tesla has worked on Optimus for years and China’s XPENG recently had its IRON humanoid walk off its own production line. There is no announced product, price or release date.

stories.headline: Trump rallies in Northern Kentucky, tells voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and promises a $100 million defense investment in the state
stories.summary: President Trump held a rally of more than an hour and a half Saturday at Northern Kentucky University in Highland Heights, his second trip to the region this year, to push turnout for Republicans in the midterms. He backed U.S. Rep. Andy Barr in the Senate race and Navy SEAL veteran Ed Gallrein in the 4th Congressional District, where Gallrein beat Rep. Thomas Massie in the GOP primary after Trump campaigned for him in March. Trump again promised $5,000 checks to adults if Republicans keep Congress, and announced that the “Department of War will be investing $100 million” in drugmaker Antheia to revive a big manufacturing plant in Winchester, Kentucky. The Pentagon did not respond to the Lantern, and Gov. Andy Beshear’s office said it had no information. Trump urged supporters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” called Barr’s Democratic opponent Charles Booker “a communist lunatic,” and went after North Carolina’s Roy Cooper and Texas Democrat James Talarico. A protester who interrupted early was booed and removed; Trump said to take the person “back home to mom.” Barr thanked Trump for the Iran campaign, saying “the Ayatollah is dead, and its nuclear infrastructure is under rubble.” Kentucky absentee-ballot requests close Oct. 20 and early voting starts Oct. 29.

stories.headline: Man shot dead on a Midtown Manhattan subway platform after a dispute; gunman fled on foot
stories.summary: A man was shot and killed Saturday afternoon at the 53rd Street and Seventh Avenue subway station in Manhattan’s Theater District, an area packed with tourists and theatergoers. Police got reports of gunfire around 12:21 p.m., and the victim, described as possibly in his 30s, was pronounced dead at a hospital at 1:06 p.m. The NYPD says a man approached him on the northbound E train platform, shot him once in the chest and ran off. At a briefing, police said an argument between the two men had moved from the platform onto a train and back onto the platform, and that the attack was not random. Investigators were still working out exactly where the shots were fired, and no arrest had been made. The victim had not been named pending notification of his family. “The perpetrator should face maximum consequences from the justice system,” said Michael Kemper, the MTA’s chief security officer.

stories.headline: Apple Store staff told to warn shoppers: don’t expect to walk in and buy an iPhone Duo on launch day
stories.summary: Some Apple Store employees have been told to discourage customers from showing up on Friday, Oct. 23, hoping to buy an iPhone Duo without a pre-order, MacRumors reports. Staff were told there will likely be no Duo stock for walk-in buyers on launch day and that people coming in expecting one will be disappointed. Apple’s online store tells shoppers to check back Saturday, Oct. 24 for pickup availability, though that doesn’t promise stock either, and it’s not clear whether the guidance applies outside the U.S. Pickup reservations briefly appeared when pre-orders opened before Apple turned the option off. Supply problems with the $1,999 foldable have been reported since late August, when production reportedly ran only a few hundred units a day. When pre-orders opened this week, every U.S. configuration slipped to a Jan. 25 ship date within 30 minutes, leaving the Duo effectively sold out online through Christmas. Apple has called demand “nothing short of extraordinary.”

stories.headline: Rush postpones tonight’s San Jose show because drummer Anika Nilles has the flu; makeup date is Dec. 6
stories.summary: Rush called off Saturday night’s concert at the SAP Center in San Jose, California, because drummer Anika Nilles is sick with the flu. The band said the show is rescheduled for Dec. 6, 2026, and that all tickets will be honored. In a video, guitarist Alex Lifeson said Nilles was already in the early stages of the flu at Thursday’s first San Jose show but “managed to get through the gig,” then got much worse. “So this really sucks,” he said. “It’s flu season.” He expects her to recover in four or five days. The “Fifty Something” tour, which opened June 7 in Los Angeles, is Rush’s first in more than 10 years and its first since drummer Neil Peart died in 2020. Lifeson and Geddy Lee are joined by Nilles, a German drummer who toured with Jeff Beck in 2022, and keyboardist Loren Gold, a touring member of The Who and Chicago. The band plays two sets a night drawn from more than 40 Rush songs.

stories.headline: Repeated Houthi strikes on Riyadh’s airport show how much stronger Yemen’s rebels have become despite a decade of air raids
stories.summary: Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels have struck Saudi Arabia’s main international airport in Riyadh several times in recent weeks and seized territory near a key shipping chokepoint, the AP reports. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, the U.S., Britain and Israel have all bombed the Houthis at different points over the last decade, and the group has come out stronger each time. A 2024 U.N. experts’ report estimated Houthi fighters had grown to as many as 350,000, up from about 30,000 in 2015. They have ballistic and cruise missiles and drones that can reach every Gulf state and Israel, and a recent report found them trying to buy Chinese parts used in precision-guided missiles with a range of about 1,200 miles. Iran denies arming them. The Houthis mostly sat out the first months of the Iran war but resumed attacks on Saudi Arabia in July and declared a blockade on Saudi shipping. The Saudis have struggled to stop the attacks with high-end U.S. interceptors that are in short supply, the anti-Houthi ground forces in Yemen are divided, and the U.S. appears keen to stay out. A senior Saudi diplomat says Iran is encouraging the escalation.

stories.headline: The Army is buying drone-killing lasers that cost under $10 a shot in a $464.8 million deal
stories.summary: The Army is moving to field a high-energy laser that shoots down drones for less than $10 a shot. AeroVironment won a $464.8 million contract in September for its LOCUST X3 laser, which the Army calls its first contract to produce a high-energy laser weapon. Army officials said at this month’s AUSA meeting in Washington that the first LOCUST X3 could be ready to counter drones by early 2028. The laser runs on electricity, so its “magazine” regenerates from the power supply. “We’re moving from science fiction to science reality,” said John Garrity, AeroVironment’s vice president of directed energy. He said each shot costs “less than a cup of coffee” in power, compared with the $500,000 to $1 million missiles now often fired at drones that cost a few thousand dollars. “Even though we’re successful in taking those out, we’re still losing,” he said. Garrity said a laser’s upfront cost is about the same as other counter-drone weapons and comes out ahead after a single kill. At the AUSA show, a hybrid truck from California chassis maker Harbinger powered a LOCUST X3 at American Rheinmetall’s booth, showing how the weapon could be run in the field.

stories.headline: Connecticut’s Secretary of the State was one of the targets of the suspicious powder letters sent to election offices nationwide
stories.summary: Connecticut’s Secretary of the State says her Hartford office was the intended target of one of the suspicious letters the FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating around the country. Federal authorities intercepted the Connecticut letter before it arrived. Some of the mailings to election offices held a powdery substance, but preliminary tests in several states found nothing hazardous. Election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma were evacuated Tuesday after workers opened envelopes with white powder. Before learning Connecticut had been targeted, the office reminded town election officials of safe mail-handling procedures. “I’m relieved that the substances tested so far have not been hazardous, but these incidents are still deplorable,” Secretary Stephanie Thomas said. “No one should have to fear for their safety simply because they’re doing their jobs.” Thomas also joined the National Association of Secretaries of State and the state election directors’ group in a joint statement condemning the mailings. Her office says it remains in close contact with the FBI and other law enforcement agencies, less than three weeks before Election Day.

stories.headline: Jets activate rookie WR Omar Cooper Jr. off injured reserve and elevate LB Jaden Keller for Sunday at New England
stories.summary: The Jets moved first-round rookie wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. from injured reserve to the 53-man roster Saturday, so he will play Sunday against the Patriots in Foxborough. They also elevated linebacker Jaden Keller from the practice squad. Cooper hurt his ankle in the Week 1 win over Tennessee after only five snaps. One of those snaps was a 30-yard catch-and-run that set up the opening-drive touchdown. He has missed the four games since. Sunday will be only his second NFL game. He had 69 catches for 937 yards and 13 touchdowns at Indiana last season. Keller, an undrafted rookie from Virginia Tech, has played 38 special-teams snaps over the last two games. Sunday will be his third straight game for the Jets. He had 10 tackles in the preseason after joining the practice squad Aug. 31.

stories.headline: Former U.S. ambassador Morse Tan is stuck in South Korea and on trial for defamation over a speech he gave in Washington
stories.summary: Morse Tan, who served as ambassador-at-large for global criminal justice in President Trump’s first term, appeared in a Seoul court Friday on criminal defamation charges brought on behalf of South Korean President Lee Jae Myung. The case stems from a June 2025 talk at the National Press Club in Washington on alleged fraud in South Korea’s presidential election. Answering a question there, Tan repeated old allegations that Lee was involved in a violent crime as a teenager and spent time in juvenile detention. South Korean prosecutors say those claims are false. A second charge covers remarks Tan made in South Korea in July 2025. He has been barred from leaving the country since he arrived in May. Tan is a constitutional-law professor and former dean of Liberty University’s law school. He pleaded not guilty, calls the case “political lawfare” and says criminal defamation “does not exist in the U.S.” South Korea’s embassy says the case follows due process. The State Department declined to discuss specifics. Tan could face prison if convicted.

stories.headline: TikTok permanently bans the account for Alex Gibney’s “Musk” documentary, citing political-policy violations
stories.summary: TikTok has permanently suspended the promotional account for “Musk,” Alex Gibney’s unflattering documentary about Elon Musk, which runs three hours and 52 minutes. According to The Hollywood Reporter, distributor Bleecker Street was told Friday that the ban was coming because of the “level of severity with political-policy violations,” and that “some violations trigger immediate suspension.” TikTok has not said which rule the account broke. The film opened nationwide Friday after a limited preview. Last month YouTube, Meta, X and TikTok all turned down ads for it. Google and Meta later reversed course, calling it an error, but TikTok and X did not. X has also refused to take Bleecker Street ads for its other films. Gizmodo points out that Oracle, controlled by Larry Ellison, owns about 15% of the consortium that runs TikTok’s U.S. business, and Ellison’s ties to Musk come up in the film. Gizmodo also notes that political content is everywhere on TikTok, and that the platform’s special rules for “political accounts” cover governments, politicians and parties, not films.

stories.headline: Nearly 12-foot alligator drags a 71-year-old fisherman into a Florida pond and kills him
stories.summary: A 71-year-old man fishing at a park in Winter Garden, Florida, was pulled into the water and killed by a nearly 12-foot alligator Friday evening, according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. Wildlife officials identified him as Steve Hamilton. The attack happened around 5 p.m. at Dr. Bradford Memorial Park, west of Orlando. The park has several small ponds that connect to Lake Apopka and is so well known for alligators that it has a crossing called Gator Bridge. Police said Hamilton was standing on shore when the alligator grabbed him. Trappers removed an 11-foot, 8-inch alligator from the scene. “Lake Apopka has tons of alligators in it,” Winter Garden Police Capt. Michael Mason said. “It looks like it’s docile… but it can be dangerous.” Hamilton is the second person killed by an alligator in Florida this year. Florida usually sees about a dozen attacks a year, and the FWC has counted 32 fatal attacks since 1948, never more than three in a single year.

stories.headline: Al Jourgensen says Ministry “has run its course” as the final album lands Oct. 30 and a goodbye tour hits 2027
stories.summary: Ministry founder Al Jourgensen says the industrial-metal band is done after one last album and farewell tour. “I just think that Ministry has run its course,” he told Hit Parader. “I’m glad it was here when it was here.” Ministry’s 17th and final studio album, “Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery),” comes out Oct. 30 on Cleopatra Records. Jourgensen, 68, called it “a culmination of 40 years of the same elements” and “a good one to go out on.” He said he is “not enthused about continuing to keep doing this kind of music or music in general.” Jourgensen says he only ever wanted to teach history and that Ministry “kept dragging me in,” comparing himself to Michael Corleone in “The Godfather Part III.” The album closes with “We’re Still Here,” a final collaboration with former member Paul Barker. The “Goodbye Europe” tour with Die Krupps starts in April 2027, and a full U.S. run follows. Ministry started in Chicago in 1981 and hit its peak with “The Land Of Rape And Honey,” “The Mind Is A Terrible Thing To Taste” and 1992’s Grammy-nominated “Psalm 69.”

stories.headline: A new Canon patent includes an RF 70-200mm f/2L IS design, a full stop faster than any 70-200 Canon sells
stories.summary: A Japanese patent application from Canon (JP 2026-168807) contains about a dozen optical designs for fast zooms, and one of them is an RF 70-200mm f/2L IS. That would be a full stop brighter than Canon’s f/2.8 versions and a natural partner for the RF 28-70mm f/2L. Canon Rumors says the design uses 23 elements in 8 groups, including 6 aspheric surfaces, and appears to zoom and focus internally. Its optical length is about 220mm before adding the flange distance. The EF 200mm f/2L prime was 210mm long as a complete lens. The patent’s real focus is a three-group focusing system. One main group does most of the work, and two lighter groups move only slightly to correct field curvature, which keeps the motors small and the lens compact. Other designs in the filing include zooms faster than f/2, such as a 50-85mm f/1.4. Canon Rumors cautions that patents often never become products. It says there is “a very small chance” a 70-200 f/2 reaches stores and guesses one would cost $6,000 to $8,000.
